name: Islam: Sunni
line: Remember God through the day, give what is due and trust what you cannot control.

quote.text: So truly where there is hardship there is also ease; truly where there is hardship there is also ease.
quote.source: Surah 94, verses 5 and 6, trans. M. A. S. Abdel Haleem

quotes.text: God does not burden any soul with more than it can bear.
quotes.source: Surah 2, verse 286, trans. M. A. S. Abdel Haleem

quotes.text: People, We created you all from a single man and a single woman, and made you into races and tribes so that you should get to know one another.
quotes.source: Surah 49, verse 13, trans. M. A. S. Abdel Haleem

quotes.text: None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
quotes.source: Hadith related by al-Bukhari and Muslim; number 13 in al-Nawawi’s Forty Hadith

quotes.text: Actions are judged by intentions, and everyone will have what they intended.
quotes.source: Hadith related by al-Bukhari and Muslim; number 1 in al-Nawawi’s Forty Hadith

quotes.text: There is no compulsion in religion.
quotes.source: Surah 2, verse 256, trans. M. A. S. Abdel Haleem

words.usage: From the same root as salam, peace. A Muslim is one who surrenders.
The Arabic word for the one God, used by Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews as well.
The central teaching. God is one, without partner, child or likeness.
The revelation given to Muhammad over twenty-three years. It is God’s speech, and it is recited aloud more than it is read silently.
The example of the Prophet: what he said, did and approved. Sunnis take their name from it.
A saying or action of the Prophet handed down through a named chain of narrators, graded for reliability.
There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God. Saying it with conviction makes one a Muslim.
Performed five times a day facing Mecca, with standing, bowing and prostration.
An annual payment of one fortieth of savings to those in need. It is a right the poor hold over the rich.
No food, drink or sex from dawn to sunset through the month of Ramadan.
The journey to Mecca once in a lifetime for those who can manage it.
Belief in God, the angels, the scriptures, the prophets, the last day and the divine decree.
To worship God as though you see Him, for though you do not see Him, He sees you.
Careful awareness of God that makes a person guard their conduct. The Qur’an calls it the best provision.
Repeating phrases that recall God, on the fingers or on a string of beads.
Personal prayer in one’s own words and language, at any time.
The purpose formed in the heart before an act. It decides the act’s worth.
Steadiness in hardship and in doing right. The Qur’an says God is with those who have it.
Thankfulness shown in the heart, on the tongue and in how blessings are used.
Doing what you can and leaving the outcome. The saying goes: tie your camel, then trust.
The first quality of God named in the Qur’an. The Prophet is described as a mercy to the worlds.
Any good freely given. A smile counts, and so does removing something harmful from the road.
The worldwide body of Muslims, of every nation and colour.
Called aloud from the mosque five times a day by a human voice.
Washing the hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet before prayer.
A mosque. The Prophet said that the whole earth had been made a place of prayer.
Said before eating, travelling, working or beginning anything.
Thanks, said after eating, on good news and in answer to how are you.
Added to any statement about the future, as a reminder of who decides it.
The greeting. The reply is wa alaykum as-salam: and upon you, peace.

practices.name: Five pauses
practices.instructions: Mark the five moments at which Muslims pray: before sunrise, just after midday, in the late afternoon, just after sunset and when night has fallen. Look up the times for your town. At each one stop what you are doing for two minutes. Stand, be still and turn your attention away from your concerns toward what is greater than you. If you are Muslim, pray. If you are a guest, simply stand in silence, give thanks and return to the day.
practices.why: The five daily prayers are the second pillar and the backbone of Muslim life. They cut the day into portions so that no stretch of it passes without remembrance. This guest’s version keeps the rhythm and leaves the rite to those whose it is.
variations: Wash your hands and face with care before each pause.
Begin with the dawn pause alone and add one each week.
Listen to the call to prayer at one of the five times.

practices.name: State your intention
practices.instructions: Before the day’s main work, and before any act that matters, stop and name your intention to yourself. Whom is this for? What good do I mean by it? If the honest answer is to be seen, to win or to get even, either correct the aim or leave the act alone. Begin with the words in the name of God, or with a plain statement of purpose.
practices.why: The first hadith in the best known collections is that actions are judged by intentions. Scholars called it a third of all knowledge. An ordinary act, done for a good reason, becomes worship.
variations: Say bismillah before eating, driving and opening your laptop.
Re-check your intention halfway through a long task.
At night, recall one act and ask what it was really for.

practices.name: Thirty-three times three
practices.instructions: Sit for five minutes. On the joints of your fingers count out thirty-three repetitions of a phrase of wonder, such as how perfect, then thirty-three of a phrase of thanks, such as all praise and thanks, then thirty-three of a phrase of greatness, such as greater than all this. Muslims say subhanAllah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar. Use those or your own. Let the mind rest on the meaning.
practices.why: This sequence of ninety-nine is recited after each prayer on the Prophet’s recommendation. Remembrance is called the polish of the heart.
variations: Through the day answer how are you with a sincere thanks.
Walk and repeat one phrase in step.

practices.name: Give every day
practices.instructions: Give something away every day. Money to someone who needs it is best, in secret if you can. If you have none to spare, give something else: help with a load, a word of encouragement, a visit, water for an animal, a stone moved off the path. Once in the Onda work out what one fortieth of your savings would be, and consider giving it.
practices.why: Zakat, the third pillar, is fixed at 2.5 per cent of saved wealth a year. Beyond it lies sadaqa, open-ended generosity. The Prophet said that every joint of the body owes a charity each day.
variations: Give to a relative or neighbour first, as the tradition advises.
Set up a standing gift, however small.

practices.name: The night account
practices.instructions: Before sleep, call yourself to account before you are called. Go through the day. For what went well, say thanks. For what went wrong, admit it, ask forgiveness and decide what you will put right with any person you wronged. Then put tomorrow in other hands: I have done what I could, and the rest is not mine to carry. Lie down in peace.
practices.why: The caliph Umar is credited with the saying: call yourselves to account before you are called to account. Turning back in repentance, tawba, is open at every moment, and trust in God is what allows sleep.
variations: Read a few verses of the Qur’an in translation first.
Forgive everyone who wronged you today before closing your eyes.
Rise a little before dawn one day and sit in the quiet.

tasks.name: Fast from dawn to sunset one day this week, if your health allows
tasks.meta: Then break the fast with water and dates, with others

tasks.name: Greet everyone you meet today with a wish of peace
Read Surah 93, The Morning Brightness, and Surah 94, Relief
tasks.meta: Read · two short chapters of comfort

tasks.name: Listen to Surah ar-Rahman recited by Abdul Basit Abdus Samad
tasks.meta: Listen · the chapter of the All-Merciful

tasks.name: Look at a page of the Blue Qur’an
tasks.meta: Art · gold Kufic script on indigo

tasks.name: Visit a mosque on an open day or outside prayer times
tasks.meta: Travel · dress modestly, take off your shoes

tasks.name: Journal: what did you worry about that was never yours to control?
Stewardship: what has been placed in your care?
Remove something harmful from a path or a street
Smile at someone: it counts as charity
Break your hunger with a date and a glass of water
Dab on a little scent before you go out
Step outside and find the moon
Drink a glass of water and pause for a minute to be thankful
Say salaam to someone you do not know
Read a short surah slowly, or lines you love

rules.why: At dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night, be still for two minutes and remember what is greater than you.
Before each task say what it is for. If the purpose is poor, change it.
Money, food, effort or a kind word. Give quietly.
No backbiting, no mockery, no lies. The Prophet tied this directly to faith.
Keep a clear head for the length of the Onda, and eat with thanks and without waste.

rules.text: Be good to parents, kin and neighbours
rules.why: Contact one of them today. The neighbour’s rights were stressed so often that the Prophet thought they might inherit.

read.title: The Qur’an: A New Translation
read.creator: trans. M. A. S. Abdel Haleem
read.why: Clear modern English by an Egyptian scholar who knows the text by heart. Start with the short chapters at the back and with chapters 1, 12, 19 and 55.

read.title: An-Nawawi’s Forty Hadith
read.creator: Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi; many translations
read.why: Forty-two short sayings of the Prophet chosen to hold the essentials of the religion. The first book many Muslim children memorise.

read.title: Muhammad: His Life Based on the Earliest Sources
read.creator: Martin Lings
read.why: The Prophet’s life told as a narrative from the early Arabic biographies. Loved by Muslim readers.

read.title: Islam: A Short History
read.creator: Karen Armstrong
read.why: Two hundred pages from Mecca to the modern world, written for the general reader.

read.title: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
read.creator: Malcolm X with Alex Haley
read.why: The chapter on his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964, where he prayed beside people of every colour, is one of the great accounts of the hajj.

read.title: The Travels of Ibn Battuta
read.creator: Ibn Battuta, abridged by Tim Mackintosh-Smith
read.why: A Moroccan jurist spends thirty years crossing the Muslim world from Mali to China and finds a mosque, a judge and a welcome almost everywhere.

watch.title: The Message
watch.creator: Moustapha Akkad
watch.why: The rise of Islam told without ever showing or voicing the Prophet, in keeping with Muslim practice. Approved in its day by scholars of al-Azhar.

watch.title: Le Grand Voyage
watch.creator: Ismaël Ferroukhi
watch.why: An ageing Moroccan father makes his French-born son drive him from Provence to Mecca. A road film about faith between generations.

watch.title: Inside Mecca
watch.creator: Anisa Mehdi, National Geographic
watch.why: Three pilgrims from South Africa, Malaysia and the United States are followed through the hajj by a Muslim crew.

watch.title: Malcolm X
watch.creator: Spike Lee
watch.why: Denzel Washington in the title role. The hajj sequence was filmed in Mecca itself by a second unit.

listen.title: Qur’an recitation
listen.creator: Abdul Basit Abdus Samad
listen.why: The Egyptian reciter with the long breath, heard in homes and taxis from Morocco to Indonesia. Try Surah ar-Rahman or the short chapters.

listen.title: The call to prayer
listen.creator: Muezzins of Cairo, Istanbul, Mecca and Medina
listen.why: The same Arabic words everywhere, in local melodic styles. First called by Bilal, a freed Ethiopian slave.

listen.title: Tala al-Badru Alayna
listen.creator: Traditional
listen.why: The full moon has risen over us: the song with which the people of Medina are said to have welcomed the Prophet.

listen.title: Qasidat al-Burda
listen.creator: Imam al-Busiri; many recordings
listen.why: The Poem of the Cloak in praise of the Prophet, sung at gatherings across the Sunni world.

art.title: The Dome of the Rock
art.creator: Jerusalem
art.why: The oldest surviving Islamic monument: an octagon under a golden dome, with the earliest dated Qur’anic inscriptions running round the inside in mosaic.

art.title: The Blue Qur’an
art.creator: Probably Kairouan, Tunisia, or Spain
art.why: Gold letters on parchment dyed deep indigo. Leaves are in Tunis, New York, Doha and other collections.

art.title: The Qur’an of Ibn al-Bawwab
art.creator: Baghdad; Chester Beatty Library, Dublin
art.why: The earliest dated Qur’an in a rounded cursive hand, by the calligrapher who perfected proportioned script.

art.title: The Alhambra
art.creator: Granada, Spain
art.why: Palace walls covered in geometry, carved plaster and the repeated phrase: there is no victor but God.

eat.title: Dates and water
eat.creator: An odd number of dates
eat.why: How the Prophet broke his fast, and how most Muslims still do at sunset in Ramadan.

eat.title: Harira
eat.creator: Tomato, lentil and chickpea soup with herbs
eat.why: The soup that opens the evening meal in Ramadan across Morocco.

eat.title: Biryani or kabsa
eat.creator: Spiced rice with meat, cooked in one pot
eat.why: A dish for feeding many people from one tray, at weddings and at the two festivals.

eat.title: Lamb shared in three parts
eat.creator: At the festival of sacrifice
eat.why: The meat is divided: a third for the household, a third for relatives and neighbours and a third for the poor.

drink.title: Mint tea
drink.creator: Green tea with fresh mint and sugar
drink.why: The drink of welcome from Morocco to the Sahel. Refusing the first glass is impolite.

drink.title: Arabic coffee
drink.creator: Lightly roasted, with cardamom, in small cups
drink.why: Poured for guests with the left hand holding the pot. Coffee drinking began among Sufis in Yemen who wanted to stay awake for night prayer.

drink.title: Laban or ayran
drink.creator: Salted yogurt drink
drink.why: Cooling, and common at the meal that breaks the fast.

customs.title: Right hand, and bismillah
customs.creator: At table
customs.why: Food is taken with the right hand after saying in the name of God, and the meal ends with praise be to God.

customs.title: Shoes off, modest dress
customs.creator: In mosques and many homes
customs.why: Prayer halls are carpeted for prostration. Visitors cover arms and legs, and women are often asked to cover their hair.

customs.title: Blessing the Prophet
customs.creator: Peace be upon him
customs.why: Muslims add this phrase whenever they mention Muhammad, and they do not depict him.

customs.title: Friday
customs.creator: The day of congregation
customs.why: At midday on Friday men are obliged, and women welcome, to pray together at the mosque and hear a sermon.

games.title: Shatranj
games.creator: Board game · Persia and the Arab world
games.why: The older form of chess. Players at the caliphs’ court in Baghdad, such as al-Adli and as-Suli, wrote the first books of openings and problems.

games.title: Mancala
games.creator: Board game · Africa and the Middle East
games.why: Seeds sown round rows of pits. The name is Arabic, from a word for moving. Played from Syria to Zanzibar.

games.title: Engare
games.creator: Video game · Mahdi Bahrami
games.why: A puzzle game from Iran in which moving shapes trace the repeating patterns of Islamic geometric art. It ends as a tool for drawing your own.

festivals.title: Ramadan
festivals.creator: The ninth lunar month; it moves about eleven days earlier each year
festivals.why: A month of fasting from dawn to sunset, extra night prayers and reading the whole Qur’an. Evenings are sociable and generous.

festivals.title: Eid al-Fitr
festivals.creator: The first day after Ramadan
festivals.why: The festival of breaking the fast. A charity is paid for every member of the household before the morning prayer. New clothes, visits and sweets.

festivals.title: Eid al-Adha
festivals.creator: The 10th of the twelfth month
festivals.why: The festival of sacrifice, recalling Abraham, on the day pilgrims at Mecca complete the central rites of the hajj.

festivals.title: The Prophet’s birthday (Mawlid)
festivals.creator: The 12th of the third month
festivals.why: Kept with poetry, processions and sweets in much of the Sunni world. Some Muslims do not celebrate it.

places.title: Mecca and Medina
places.creator: Saudi Arabia
places.why: The Kaaba, toward which all Muslims pray, and the Prophet’s mosque and tomb. Mecca and the sacred centre of Medina are open to Muslims only.

places.title: Al-Azhar Mosque and Islamic Cairo
places.creator: Cairo, Egypt
places.why: A mosque and university founded in 970 that became the leading seat of Sunni learning. Visitors are welcome outside prayer times.

places.title: The Great Mosque of Kairouan
places.creator: Tunisia
places.why: Founded in 670 and rebuilt in the ninth century. One of the oldest mosques in the world, with a forest of reused Roman columns.

places.title: The Mosque-Cathedral of Córdoba
places.creator: Andalusia, Spain
places.why: Hundreds of red and white double arches from the tenth century capital of Muslim Spain, with a church set in the middle since the sixteenth.

places.title: Istiqlal Mosque
places.creator: Jakarta, Indonesia
places.why: The national mosque of the country with the most Muslims in the world, facing the Catholic cathedral across the road. Guided visits are free.

ethics.title: Justice
ethics.text: Stand firmly for justice, says the Qur’an, even against yourselves, your parents or your kin, whether the person is rich or poor.
ethics.practice: Admit you were wrong in one matter today, to the person concerned.

ethics.title: Mercy
ethics.text: Every chapter of the Qur’an but one opens in the name of God, the Lord of Mercy, the Giver of Mercy. Those who show no mercy, said the Prophet, will be shown none.
ethics.practice: Let someone off today when you could have insisted.

ethics.title: Honesty in dealings
ethics.text: Give full measure and weight. The Prophet was known as the trustworthy before he was a prophet, and a merchant who is honest is promised the company of the martyrs.
ethics.practice: Check one bill, claim or timesheet for fairness to the other side.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.text: Wealth is a trust. The one who sleeps full while a neighbour is hungry is not a believer, runs a hadith.
ethics.practice: Find out whether anyone near you is going without, and act.

ethics.title: Guarding the tongue
ethics.text: Backbiting is likened in the Qur’an to eating the flesh of one’s dead brother. Suspicion and spying are forbidden with it.
ethics.practice: Defend someone who is being talked about in their absence.

ethics.title: Kindness to parents
ethics.text: Do not say to them even a word of contempt, says the Qur’an, and lower to them the wing of humility. Paradise is said to lie at the feet of mothers.
ethics.practice: Serve a parent or an elder today without being asked.

philosophy.title: One God
philosophy.text: Tawhid is more than counting gods. If God alone is ultimate, then nothing else is: money, nation, self, fear. To surrender to the One is to be freed from serving the many.
philosophy.practice: Name the thing that actually governs your day. Would you choose it as your master?

philosophy.title: Stewardship
philosophy.text: The Qur’an says God placed humankind on earth as khalifa, a deputy or steward. The earth, the body, wealth and children are held in trust and will be answered for.
philosophy.practice: List three things in your care. Do one thing today to look after each.

philosophy.title: The natural disposition
philosophy.text: Every child is born on the fitra, a natural inclination to know God and do good. Religion is a reminder of what one already is. The human problem is forgetfulness more than corruption.
philosophy.practice: Set three reminders today of what you most want to remember.

philosophy.title: Intention
philosophy.text: Two people may do the same act and one is rewarded and the other not. What a deed is depends on why it was done. This gives ordinary life a hidden depth.
philosophy.practice: Take a routine chore and decide, before doing it, to do it as a gift.

philosophy.title: Trust and effort
philosophy.text: A man asked whether he should tie his camel or trust in God. Tie it, said the Prophet, and trust. Do everything in your power, then release the result.
philosophy.practice: Pick one worry. Do the one thing you can about it today and put the rest down.

philosophy.title: Hardship and ease
philosophy.text: The verse does not say that ease follows hardship. It says ease comes with it, and says so twice. Difficulty is treated as a test and a cleansing, never as abandonment.
philosophy.practice: Find the ease that is already inside a present difficulty.

philosophy.title: Excellence
philosophy.text: The angel Gabriel asked the Prophet what ihsan is. He answered: to worship God as if you see Him. It means doing everything beautifully because it is seen.
philosophy.practice: Do one unobserved task today to the highest standard you can.

philosophy.title: The middle community
philosophy.text: The Qur’an calls Muslims a community of the middle way. The Prophet rebuked followers who vowed to fast every day, pray all night and never marry. Moderation is the norm.
philosophy.practice: Notice where you run to an extreme, and move one step toward the middle.

dayThemes: No more than you can bear

intro: Islam is the religion of about two billion people, nearly a quarter of humanity. Its name means willing surrender to God, and it shares a root with the word for peace. Muslims understand it as the same faith taught by Abraham, Moses and Jesus, restored and completed in the revelation given to Muhammad, a merchant of Mecca, between the years 610 and 632.

That revelation is the Qur’an, which Muslims hold to be the speech of God in Arabic, memorised and recited ever since. Its message is the oneness of God, who is merciful and just, the moral responsibility of every person, the reality of a final reckoning and the duty to care for orphans, the poor and the traveller. Alongside it stands the Sunnah, the example of the Prophet, preserved in thousands of reports called hadith.

Practice rests on five pillars. The testimony of faith. Prayer five times a day, facing Mecca. An annual due of one fortieth of savings for those in need. Fasting from dawn to sunset through the month of Ramadan. And the pilgrimage to Mecca once in a lifetime for those able. Around these has grown a detailed way of life covering food, family, trade and manners, worked out by jurists and known as the sharia, the path to water.

Sunni is short for the people of the Prophet’s way and of the community. The name goes back to a disagreement after the Prophet’s death about who should lead. Those who became the Sunnis accepted the leaders chosen by the community, beginning with his close companion Abu Bakr. Those who became the Shia held that leadership belonged to his cousin and son-in-law Ali and his descendants. The two share the Qur’an, the pillars and most of their practice. Shia Islam has its own Onda in this app.

Sunni Islam has no pope and no priesthood. Authority lies with scholars, and four schools of law, the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali, are recognised as equally valid. From the eighth century onward Sunni scholars built one of the great intellectual traditions of the world in law, theology, grammar, medicine and mathematics, and the mystical path of the Sufis grew up within it.

This Onda borrows the shape of a Muslim day: five pauses at the times of prayer, a stated intention, remembrance on the fingers, daily giving and an account at night. If you are Muslim, it may refresh what you know. If you are a guest, you are not asked to perform the ritual prayer or to say the testimony of faith, which are acts of commitment. A mosque visit is usually easy to arrange, and you will be welcome.
guide.origin: Mecca and Medina in western Arabia; today from Senegal to Indonesia and worldwide
guide.era: The Prophet Muhammad lived from about 570 to 632. Sunni Islam is the faith of about 85 to 90 per cent of Muslims

figures.name: The Prophet Muhammad
figures.bio: Born in Mecca and orphaned early. He received the first revelation at forty in a cave on Mount Hira, emigrated to Medina in 622 and by his death had united Arabia.

figures.name: Khadija bint Khuwaylid
figures.bio: A wealthy merchant who employed and then married Muhammad. She was the first to believe him and supported him with her fortune.

figures.name: Abu Bakr
figures.bio: The Prophet’s closest friend and father-in-law, and the first caliph. He held the community together after the Prophet’s death.

figures.name: Umar ibn al-Khattab
figures.bio: The second caliph, under whom Muslim rule reached Egypt and Persia. Remembered for plain living and strict justice.

figures.name: Aisha bint Abi Bakr
figures.bio: A wife of the Prophet and one of the chief transmitters of his sayings. Companions and later scholars came to her for rulings.

figures.name: Abu Hanifa
figures.bio: A silk merchant of Kufa and founder of the most widely followed school of law. He refused a judgeship and died in prison.

figures.name: Muhammad al-Bukhari
figures.bio: From Bukhara. He travelled for sixteen years sifting reports of the Prophet and kept some seven thousand in the collection Sunnis rank next to the Qur’an.

figures.name: Fatima al-Fihri
figures.bio: A merchant’s daughter who used her inheritance to found the Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez in 859. It grew into what is often called the oldest university still operating.

figures.name: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali
figures.bio: The most celebrated teacher in Baghdad, who left his post after a crisis of doubt and wrote The Revival of the Religious Sciences, joining law, theology and the inner life.

figures.name: Ibn Battuta
figures.bio: A jurist from Tangier who set out for Mecca at twenty-one and kept travelling for nearly thirty years.

history.detail: In a cave outside Mecca the angel Gabriel commands Muhammad: recite. He begins to preach the oneness of God, and the city’s leaders turn against him.
Muhammad and his followers move to Medina, where he founds a community and makes a pact with its tribes, including its Jews. The Muslim calendar starts from this year.
Mecca surrenders almost without bloodshed and the Kaaba is cleared of idols. In 632 the Prophet makes his only pilgrimage, preaches that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, and dies in Medina.
Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali lead in turn. Muslim armies take Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia. The period ends in civil war.
Under Uthman an official written text is compiled from the reciters and the early written pieces, and copies are sent to the main cities.
A dynasty ruling from Damascus extends the empire from Spain to the Indus. The Dome of the Rock is built.
The capital moves to Baghdad. Greek, Persian and Indian learning is translated, and the sciences of law, hadith and theology mature.
Abu Hanifa, Malik, al-Shafi’i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal work out methods for deriving law. Their four schools become the framework of Sunni practice.
Al-Bukhari, Muslim and four others compile the hadith collections that Sunnis treat as canonical.
Madrasas spread from Baghdad. Al-Ghazali reconciles legal learning with Sufi devotion.
The Mongols sack the city and kill the caliph. New centres of Sunni power arise in Cairo, Delhi and later Istanbul.
Traders and Sufis carry Islam into West Africa, the Indian Ocean coasts and the Malay archipelago. Mali, Timbuktu and Aceh become centres of learning.
The Turkish republic abolishes the Ottoman caliphate. The twentieth century brings colonial rule and independence, reform movements and wide debate about law, the state and modern life.

concepts.detail: Testimony, prayer, alms, fasting and pilgrimage. They are set out in a famous hadith in which the angel Gabriel questions the Prophet.
God, the angels, the revealed books, the messengers, the last day and the divine decree, both its good and its bitter.
The Qur’an is God’s word, and the Sunnah shows how the Prophet lived it. Jurists add consensus and reasoning by analogy.

Sharia is the divine will for human conduct. Fiqh is the human effort to understand it, and that effort is fallible and varied. Acts are graded from required to forbidden, with most things simply permitted.
Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali differ in method and in many details and recognise one another as sound.
God sent guidance to every people. Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus are all honoured, and Muhammad is the seal who closes the line.
Every soul will be raised and shown its deeds, down to an atom’s weight of good or evil. God’s mercy is said to outstrip His wrath.
The agreement of the community’s scholars. Sunnis cite the saying that the community will not agree on an error.
The word means striving in God’s cause. Scholars distinguish the struggle against one’s own lower self from armed defence, which is bound by strict rules.

facts.text: The Muslim year has twelve lunar months and is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan passes through every season in thirty-three years.
Millions of living people know the entire Qur’an by heart. One who does is called a hafiz, a guardian.
The country with the most Muslims is Indonesia. Most Muslims are not Arabs.
The words algebra and algorithm come from the name and the book of al-Khwarizmi, a ninth century scholar in Baghdad.
Mosques have no images of living beings. Decoration is geometry, plant forms and writing.
About two million people from nearly every country gather for the hajj each year, the men dressed in two unsewn white cloths.

sensitivity.note: Sunni Islam is the living faith of well over a billion people. This Onda borrows the rhythm and the ethics of a Muslim day. It does not ask a guest to perform the ritual prayer or to recite the testimony of faith, and it is no substitute for learning from Muslims.
requiredCaveats: Muslims differ by school of law, country and culture. Local custom is often mistaken for religion.
The Prophet is not depicted, and Muslims add a blessing when naming him. The Qur’an in Arabic is handled with ritual care.
Muslims are frequent targets of prejudice. Do not treat the acts of extremists as representative.
Fasting is optional here. Do not fast if you are ill, pregnant or have a history of disordered eating.
